headline: Pentagon plans to stream an execution live

chunks.text: The Pentagon says it will stream an execution live online for the first time. On October 8, 2026, the defense secretary said the military will {{carry out}} the death sentence of the Fort Hood shooter on December 3. The execution will [[take place]] by firing squad at Fort Hood, an [[Army base]] in Texas. If the plan {{goes ahead}}, anyone could {{tune in}}.

verbs.correct: To do something that was planned
verbs.wrong: To announce a plan in public
verbs.why: The team carries out a survey every June. Workers carry out the repairs on time. The defense secretary said the military will carry out the sentence on December 3.

verbs.wrong: To be argued about in court
verbs.why: The game goes ahead even when it is cold. Most outdoor concerts go ahead in light rain. If the plan goes ahead, anyone could watch it.

verbs.correct: To watch a show or stream
verbs.wrong: To share a link with others
verbs.why: Millions tune in to watch the final game every year. Many families tune in at eight for the evening news. If the plan goes ahead, anyone could tune in.

chunks.text: The man is a former Army [[psychiatrist]]. On November 5, 2009, he killed 13 people at the base. A [[military jury]] {{handed down}} a death sentence in August 2013. The execution is [[scheduled]] for 1 p.m., the same time as the 2009 attack. The military last used a firing squad in 1945, so the plan would {{bring that method back}} after 81 years. It would be the first public execution in the country in about 90 years.

verbs.wrong: To give a prisoner to the police
verbs.why: A judge hands down a fine for speeding. The school hands down a one-day suspension for fighting. A military jury handed down a death sentence in August 2013.

verbs.wrong: To change the rules for a trial
verbs.why: The cafe brings back its summer menu every June. Fashion often brings back old styles. The plan would bring the firing squad back after more than 80 years.

chunks.text: The defense secretary said the stream would act as a [[deterrent]]. President Trump {{signed off on}} the use of a firing squad on October 5. On October 9, a reporter asked him if he had [[approved]] the live stream. He answered, "Absolutely." On October 10, he said he would make the final decision himself. One Republican congressman {{spoke up for}} the plan. He said a public execution is what the shooter deserves.

verbs.wrong: To hire a team of lawyers
verbs.why: The manager signs off on the work schedule every week. The city signs off on plans for new parks. President Trump signed off on the use of a firing squad on October 5.

verbs.wrong: To write a new law on a topic
verbs.why: She speaks up for bike lanes at every meeting. Parents often speak up for a longer lunch break. One Republican congressman spoke up for the plan.

chunks.text: The plan {{set off}} [[strong criticism]] from Republicans and Democrats. A Republican senator called it "beyond disgusting." The top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee {{called on}} the government to [[reconsider]]. [[Rights groups]] and [[legal experts]] also {{weighed in}}. The UN human rights office said a [[broadcast]] would break the [[ban]] on torture. A law professor {{pointed out}} that Army rules [[bar]] anyone under 18 from watching an execution. He said parents who want to {{keep children away}} from the stream might challenge the plan.

verbs.why: A price increase sets off angry complaints. Rude comments often set off long debates at work. The plan set off strong criticism from both parties.

verbs.correct: To formally ask someone to act
verbs.why: Parents call on the school to add more buses. The mayor calls on people to save water every summer. A top Democrat called on the government to reconsider the plan.

verbs.wrong: To raise money for a group
verbs.why: Everyone weighs in on where to eat dinner. My sister always weighs in on paint colors. Rights groups and legal experts also weighed in on the plan.

verbs.correct: To say something others should notice
verbs.wrong: To ask a question in public
verbs.why: Teachers point out common mistakes in our reports. He often points out that the store closes early on Sundays. A law professor pointed out that Army rules bar anyone under 18 from watching an execution.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from getting near
verbs.why: Good owners keep their dogs away from chocolate. We keep our little son away from the stairs. A law professor said parents may want to keep children away from the stream.

mainIdea.s: The American military plans to show the Fort Hood shooter's execution live online in December. The defense secretary calls it a warning, but lawmakers from both parties criticized the idea.
mainIdea.why: The defense secretary sees the stream as a deterrent. The plan set off strong criticism from both parties, and rights groups also weighed in.

mainIdea.s: President Trump has made a final decision to show a soldier's execution on the internet. Most members of Congress support the plan, and rights groups have said nothing about it so far.
mainIdea.why: Close, but on October 10, Trump said he would still make the final decision himself. The plan set off strong criticism from both parties.

mainIdea.s: A court in Texas has agreed to look again at a 2009 case from an Army base in Texas. The judges will hear new evidence next spring, and families of the victims plan to attend each day.
mainIdea.why: The Pentagon plans to stream an execution live on December 3. The defense secretary said the military will carry out the sentence that day.

tf.s: The defense secretary said the military will carry out the sentence on December 3.
tf.why: He announced the date on October 8, 2026. The execution will take place at Fort Hood, an Army base in Texas.

tf.s: Under the plan, the public would not be able to tune in to the execution.
tf.why: The Pentagon plans to stream the execution live online, so anyone could tune in if the plan goes ahead.

tf.s: President Trump signed off on the use of a firing squad on October 5.
tf.why: He signed off on the firing squad that day. On October 10, he said he would make the final decision on the live stream himself.

tf.s: The UN human rights office spoke up for the plan to stream the execution.
tf.why: The UN human rights office weighed in against the plan. It said a broadcast would break the ban on torture.

tf.s: The plan set off criticism from only one political party.
tf.why: It set off strong criticism from both parties, including a Republican senator and a top Democrat.

tf.s: A law professor pointed out that Army rules bar anyone under 18 from watching an execution.
tf.why: He said parents who want to keep children away from the stream might challenge the plan.

lines.text: Did you see that the Pentagon wants to stream an execution live?
I did. It's the Fort Hood shooter, right?
Yes. The military plans to {{carry out}} the sentence on December 3.
That's the idea, if the plan {{goes ahead}}.
He {{signed off on}} the firing squad. But the live stream is still [[up in the air]].
This story really [[hit a nerve]] in Washington.
It {{set off}} criticism from both parties. A top Democrat {{called on}} the government to reconsider.
So lawmakers think it's [[a step too far]]?
Most of the ones who spoke did. One Republican congressman supports it, though.
Why does the defense secretary want it public?
He says it shows there are serious consequences for such crimes.
Legal experts and rights groups have {{weighed in}}. Some say it could break the law.
A law professor {{pointed out}} that Army rules bar anyone under 18 from watching.
[[I hear you]]. How would they {{keep kids away}} from a stream on the internet?

expressions.def: Used when something makes people feel strongly or upset
ex: His joke about money hit a nerve with his parents.

expressions.def: Something that people think is more than they can accept
ex: Asking us to work on Sundays was a step too far.
A fee for using the restroom felt like a step too far.

expressions.def: Used to show that you understand someone's point
ex: I hear you, but I still think we should leave early.
